results.api: Ndk.requests.query(filter, explicitRelays: [relay]).stream (closes after EOSE), one relay
results.crypto: libsecp256k1 (C, via rust secp256k1 0.31 in ndk's librust_lib_ndk.so, built by its build hook)
results.notes: Event verifier: RustEventVerifier() (Rust via FFI: id hash + BIP-340 in one native call). Every event goes through VerifyEventStream: Nip01Utils.isIdValid (Dart id recompute + NIP-13 PoW check) and the verifier; invalid events are dropped. It keeps an LRU of verified id/sig pairs per Ndk instance (a new Ndk per run, so nothing is reused across runs). Frames are JSON-decoded on an encoding isolate. NdkConfig: bootstrapRelays = [the relay] (connected and awaited in setup, untimed), MemCacheManager (a required parameter), log level off, and query timeout = 1 h (the default 10 s query timeout would cut the stream). The stream closes when the relay sends EOSE: that is the EOSE time. query(cacheRead: false, cacheWrite: false): with cacheWrite off ndk returns the verified stream as is, so nothing is stored (the defaults run in the ndk-cache variant). Expired events and older kind-0 versions are delivered. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: the id is computed twice (isIdValid in Dart, then again in the native call), the NIP-13 check, the frame's string length taken for relay stats, the query's returnedIds dedup set; and after connect ndk fires an unawaited NIP-11 HTTP GET (setup, but it may still be in flight). Nip01Event's constructor replaces created_at: 0 with the current time, so that valid event fails its id check and is dropped: accepted_ok is false.

results.api: WebSocketRelayDataSource + SubscriptionRepositoryImpl.subscribe + EventRepositoryImpl.eventStream/eoseStream, one relay
results.notes: EventRepositoryImpl drops events whose signature fails (EventModel.isValid = bip340.verify(pubkey, id, sig)) but never checks the id. results.api: Nostr().services.relays.init([relay]) + startEventsSubscription(request, onEose).stream, one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. A new Nostr() instance per run (Nostr.instance is a process-wide singleton whose registry drops event ids it has seen before). The relay layer does not verify: per event the harness calls NostrEvent.getEventId(...) (the library's id function, jsonEncode + SHA-256) against id, then event.isVerified() (BIP-340 only). Per-event console logging is on by default and turned off (NostrDebugOptions(isLogsEnabled: false)). The relay layer jsonDecodes each frame once. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: every raw frame string goes into an LRU set of 5000 (frame-level dedup) and onto an all-data-entities sink; every event is stored in the instance's unbounded eventsRegistry map (event-level dedup, so a new Nostr() per run); and its log strings (frame, content) are interpolated per event even with logs off.

results.api: Relay(url).connect() + relay.messages (Stream<RelayMessage>) + relay.subscribe([filter]), one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. Relay parses every frame (jsonDecode + RelayMessage.parse into Event) but does not verify: per event the harness calls event.verify() (the library's own: recomputed id, then BIP-340). Frames that fail to parse come out as stream errors and are counted as rejected.

results.api: RelayApi(relayUrl).connect() (Stream<Message>) + relay.sub([filter]), one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. Last release 2023. The relay stream delivers every event unverified (the verifying Event constructor body is commented out): per event the harness calls EventApi().getEventHash(event) (the library's id function) against event.id, then EventApi().verifySignature(event) (BIP-340). The relay picks its own random subscription id. connect() does not expose the handshake: setup waits 200 ms after it (untimed).

results.api: Nostr().pool.add(Relay(url)) + await pool.subscribe([filter], onEvent) (returns at EOSE), one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. Last release 2023. RelayPool verifies every event (Event.isValid: id recomputed; Event.isSigned: BIP-340; signature verification is on unless Nostr(disableSignatureVerification: true)). The pool hides EOSE, but pool.subscribe() awaits the relay's ack, which is the EOSE: its return is the EOSE time. Relay.connect() needs NIP-11 over https and NIPs 15+20 listed, so Relay gets a RelayInfoProvider (its public constructor parameter) that returns {supported_nips: [1, 11, 15, 20]}. Caveat: the ack wait has a hard-coded 1 min timeout that disconnects the relay, so a subscription whose EOSE takes longer than 1 min to process is cut off. Relay.connect() starts IOWebSocketChannel.connect without awaiting the handshake (the channel is private), so setup waits 200 ms after pool.add (untimed), as for nostr_tools and nostr_client. It pins bip340 ^0.0.4 (as nostr_client and nostr_dart do), whose verify serializes the public key with bigToBytes (helpers.dart:12, no left padding): for a pubkey whose first byte is 0 the BIP-340 challenge hashes 31 bytes and the valid signature fails, so every event from such a key is dropped (83 in the full corpus; fixed in bip340 0.2.0, which the ^0.0.4 constraint excludes).

results.api: Relay(url).connect() + relay.stream (Stream<Message>) + relay.subscribe(filter), one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. Last release 2023. The relay stream delivers raw jsonDecoded messages; the harness turns EVENT messages into the library's Event with Event.fromJson and calls event.verify() (BIP-340 over the id, the library's only check). Who does which half: the signature is the library's event.verify(), called by the harness; the id half is harness code, because the library has no id function: the harness recomputes SHA-256 (package:crypto) of jsonEncode([0, pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content]) (what the other Dart libraries do) and compares it with the id field, inside the run. connect() is lazy (IOWebSocketChannel.connect without awaiting the handshake): setup waits 200 ms after it (untimed). It pins bip340 ^0.0.4 (as nostr_client and nostr_dart do), whose verify serializes the public key with bigToBytes (helpers.dart:12, no left padding): for a pubkey whose first byte is 0 the BIP-340 challenge hashes 31 bytes and the valid signature fails, so every event from such a key is dropped (83 in the full corpus; fixed in bip340 0.2.0, which the ^0.0.4 constraint excludes).

results.api: dart:io WebSocket + Request(...).serialize() + Message.deserialize(frame), one relay
results.websocket: dart:io WebSocket (the library has no relay client; its examples use dart:io WebSocket)
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run (no warmup), measured after a container restart moved the run to a faster host (the Go control row took 50.7-54.5 us/event there against 63.8-66.8 for the rest of the run): read it as about 20% fast next to the other rows. The library has no WebSocket client ("transport-agnostic"), so this is a variant paired with dart:io WebSocket as in its examples. Message.deserialize parses each frame; for an EVENT it builds the Event with the default verify: true, which recomputes the id and checks the BIP-340 signature and throws on failure (counted as rejected). Library cost, named not worked around: each EVENT frame is JSON-decoded twice, once by Message.deserialize (to read the message type) and again by Event.deserialize on the same frame string. Event's constructor rejects created_at <= 0 (event.dart:132, "not a valid Unix timestamp"), so the corpus's one valid event with created_at 0 is dropped: accepted_ok is false for that reason.

results.api: Ndk.requests.query(filter, explicitRelays: [relay]).stream (closes after EOSE), one relay
results.crypto: bip340 0.3.1 + pointycastle 4.0.0 (pure Dart, on compute isolates)
results.notes: Event verifier: Bip340EventVerifier() (the documented default: pure Dart, verifies on a compute isolate). Every event goes through VerifyEventStream: Nip01Utils.isIdValid (Dart id recompute + NIP-13 PoW check) and the verifier; invalid events are dropped. It keeps an LRU of verified id/sig pairs per Ndk instance (a new Ndk per run, so nothing is reused across runs). Frames are JSON-decoded on an encoding isolate. The stream closes when the relay sends EOSE: that is the EOSE time. query(cacheRead: false, cacheWrite: false): with cacheWrite off ndk returns the verified stream as is, so nothing is stored (the defaults run in the ndk-cache variant). Expired events and older kind-0 versions are delivered. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: the id is computed twice (isIdValid in VerifyEventStream and again inside Bip340EventVerifier.verify), the NIP-13 check, the frame's string length taken for relay stats, the query's returnedIds dedup set; and after connect ndk fires an unawaited NIP-11 HTTP GET (setup, but it may still be in flight). Nip01Event's constructor replaces created_at: 0 with the current time, so that valid event fails its id check and is dropped: accepted_ok is false.
